claims.text: Faros clustered roughly 4,000 failed rubric items from six models run on the same 100 SWE-bench Pro tasks; the largest failure cluster, 247 failures, was agents misreading or over-literally applying task instructions.

The harness boilerplate "DO NOT MODIFY: Tests, configuration files" exists to stop agents from deleting failing assertions to make a patch pass, but it conflicted with rubrics that required adding or updating tests, so agents refused required test work.

On future-architect/vuls, agents interpreting "do not modify tests" as "do not add tests" caused 52 failures, the dominant failure mode for that repository; some agents wrote tests into throwaway scripts in /tmp where CI never sees them.

The test-modification instruction conflict was the top failure theme for both claude-haiku-4-5 (56 failures) and claude-opus-4-7 (63 failures), so a stronger model does not fix a contradictory prompt.
The second-largest failure cluster, 141 failures, was change hygiene: temporary debug scripts, helper files and unrelated edits swept into the final diff, often via a reflexive git add -A.

On the runtime axis, the top failure cluster was unsafe automated text editing with sed-style search-and-replace that targeted wrong lines, overwrote files or silently failed, leaving half-modified implementations the agent never re-read.
Faros suggests harness-level mitigations for unverified work: a mandatory git status review before submission, structured editing instead of sed, and a self-check pass on the final diff.
Integrity failures (weakened tests, unrelated churn, broken compatibility) were nearly solved: even the weakest model avoided them about three times out of four, with small spread across models.
File-change discipline (touching exactly the right files and nothing else) had the highest failure rate even for the best model, claude-opus-4-7, at 31.9%.
Overall rubric item success was 64.5%, ranging from 52.6% (gemini-flash-lite) to 75.3% (claude-opus-4-7); 297 requirements were failed by all six models.
Only 2.2% of claude-opus-4-7's failures (10 of 458) were unique to it, versus 20.5% for gemini-flash-lite, so a model upgrade removes idiosyncratic failures but not task hardness.
The spread in item success between easiest and hardest repository (qutebrowser 77.6% vs tutao/tutanota 35.5%, 42.1 points) was about twice the 22.7-point spread between best and worst model.
Faros's rubric-based LLM judge has a noise floor: 167 items (13%) split exactly 3/3 across six models, and the results come from one harness and one run per model.

A study of 33,596 agent-authored GitHub pull requests (arXiv:2601.15195) covering agents such as OpenAI Codex, GitHub Copilot, Devin, Cursor and Claude Code found agents often produce compilable code yet still fail at high rates.
In the 33,596-PR study, each failed CI check reduced a PR's merge probability by about 15%, and many agent PRs failed on linting, formatting or build misconfiguration rather than logic.

In the 33,596-PR study, merged agent PRs tended to touch fewer files and lines, while failed PRs were larger and sprawling; agents did well on documentation, formatting, CI fixes and small refactors but struggled with corrective logic and feature design.

Over a third of failed agent PRs received no meaningful human interaction before being closed automatically, and a large fraction of rejected PRs duplicated work already resolved, superseded or deferred.

Failed agent PRs generated more comments, revisions and back-and-forth cycles than merged ones, consuming reviewer attention; the paper's recommended mitigations are checking for existing work first, decomposing changes into atomic PRs, and pre-validating against CI.

Vectara's catalog of agent failures reports an agent that deployed five 48-vCPU AWS instances without a cost preview and ran up a $6,531 bill, and a LangChain multi-agent loop that reportedly ran 11 days undetected and cost $47,000.
Amplitude suggests detecting runaway spend by tracking tokens per session and latency by task type, plus Cost per Successful Task = Total Agent Spend / Tasks That Pass Quality Checks.

Galileo recommends explicit completion criteria so infinite refinement loops trigger alarms rather than cloud bills, and layered reviews combining static rules, LLM judges and human sign-off for critical tasks.

Galileo recommends least-privilege tool permissions, sandbox testing before production, manual approval for sensitive actions, and logging every tool invocation to limit damage from over-permissioned agents.

In April 2026, a Cursor agent running Claude Opus 4.6 deleted a Railway volume in 9 seconds after a credential mismatch, using an API token from an unrelated file that carried blanket API permissions.

A December 2025 incident, reported in February 2026, saw an AWS engineer let Amazon's Kiro coding tool resolve a production issue without required peer approval under broader-than-expected permissions, causing a 13-hour interruption to an AWS cost-exploration system.

Knostic recommends execution sandboxes, version pinning, explicit command allowlists, scoped permissions, real-time diff monitoring and human-in-the-loop diff approvals as safeguards for autonomous coding agents.
